extracted.intended_audience: scholars and advanced students of classical mathematics and history of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Methods, reductions, and constructive criteria (using conchoids, conics, cylinders/tores, projections, polygonal approximations) for trisecting angles and duplicating the cube in classical Greek geometry. Includes algebraic equivalences and mechanical/practical remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Polygonal bounding method for π (Archimedes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximate π by inscribing and circumscribing regular polygons and calculating their perimeters (Archimedes used polygons of 96 sides to obtain bounds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perimeters of inscribed and circumscribed regular polygons to produce lower and upper bounds for the ratio of circumference to diameter. Archimedes' Measurement of a Circle Prop. 3 gives such bounds; later corrections and other works (e.g., on 'Flinthides and Cylinders') refine the approximation. Example figures and corrected readings yield bounds like 3.1416016 > π > 3.1415904 and mean approximations such as 3.141596.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexagesimal chord-table method for π (Ptolemy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Compute π from Ptolemy's Table of Chords by expressing chord lengths in sexagesimal fractions of 1/120th of the diameter and using the perimeter of the 360-sided inscribed polygon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chord subtended by 1° is given in sexagesimal (e.g., 1'2'50" in units of 1/120 of diameter). Multiply by 360 and convert to diameter units to obtain π (Ptolemy's figure 3 8'30" = 3.1416). Useful when a table of chords is available; yields a practical value for daily use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduction of angle trisection to a vevais (insertion problem)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reduce trisection of an angle to the problem of inserting a straight line of given length between two given lines so that it 'verges' toward a given point (a 'vevais' problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct auxiliary parallelogram and use the reduction described (e.g., make DE, bisect, join AG, etc.) to reduce the trisection to drawing BE of given length 2·AB between AE and AC verging to B. Once reduced, solve the vevais by conic intersections (circle and hyperbola) as Pappus prescribes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conchoid (cochloid) construction and fundamental property (Nicomedes)
rubrics_metrics.description: A conchoid is a curve constructed mechanically with a base line (ruler), a pole, and a fixed intercept (distance); polar equation r = a + h sec θ (in modern form). Its fundamental property: along any radius vector from the pole, the length intercepted between the curve and the base line is constant (the fixed distance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the conchoid when one of the two given lines in a vevais is a straight line: intersect the other line with an appropriate conchoid (pole = fixed point to which the inserted straight line must verge, distance = given segment length). Nicomedes' mechanical device (rulers, peg sliding in a slot) yields the curve in practice; Pappus notes practitioners sometimes found the intercept by trial instead of drawing the full curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of the conchoid depending on parameters
rubrics_metrics.description: A conchoid takes three forms depending on the relation between the fixed intercept a and the pole distance h: (1) a > h: curve has a loop; (2) a = h: curve has a cusp at the pole; (3) a < h: curve has no double point. In every case the base is an asymptote in each direction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate variety for the geometric configuration of the vevais (loop/cusp/no-double-point). Pappus' 'first', 'second', 'third', 'fourth' cochloids likely correspond to these parameter regimes and practical variations in construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence of vevais to a cubic equation
rubrics_metrics.description: The geometric vevais problem (inserting a line of given length between two lines with a verge condition) is algebraically equivalent to solving a cubic equation obtained by eliminating variables from the conic relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pappus' reduction yields simultaneous relations (e.g., xy = ab and another quadratic-type relation) that eliminate to a cubic in the unknown. Thus trisecting an angle by these methods implicitly requires solving a cubic; trisection cannot be achieved by straightedge-and-compass because it generally requires a cubic solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyperbola–circle intersection method for vevais (Pappus)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the general parallelogram insertion problem, the unknown point G lies simultaneously on a circle (center B with given radius) and on a hyperbola (with given asymptotes determined by the parallelogram); their intersection gives G (and hence the required inserted segment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct the hyperbola determined by the parallelogram's parameters and the circle of given radius; their intersection solves the vevais. Euclidean results about complements of parallelograms are used to derive the hyperbola. This is a standard way to reduce vevais-type constructions to conic intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct conic constructions for angle trisection (Pappus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct suitable conics (hyperbolas with specific transverse/conjugate axes or other conics) whose intersection with the given circle or chords yields a point P such that OP trisects the given central angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: divide chord AB at G with AG = 2·GB and construct a hyperbola with AG as transverse axis and conjugate axis √3·AG; intersection with the circle gives P with OP trisecting the angle. Another method constructs a hyperbola via focus/directrix and eccentricity 2 to obtain the same hyperbola used above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of focus–directrix definition to construct conics
rubrics_metrics.description: A locus defined by the ratio of distances from a fixed point (focus) and a fixed line (directrix) equal to a constant yields a conic (ellipse, parabola, hyperbola depending on the ratio).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pappus and related authors use focus-directrix characterizations to construct hyperbolas needed for trisection or mean-proportional problems; e.g., to get a hyperbola with eccentricity 2, take S as focus and XE as directrix. Knowledge of this locus property is required for these constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archimedes' vevais-type reduction for trisection (via chord extension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given chord AB of a circle, extend AB to C so BC equals the radius; draw GO meeting circle in D,E; then arc AE equals three times arc BD; this reduces trisection of a given arc to finding an arc one-third of AE by constructing a point B such that BG equals the radius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use chord extension and parallel-chord arguments (Euclidean propositions) to transform the trisection of arc AE into a vevais problem of drawing a chord/segment with a specified length condition, solvable by conics as above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanical/trial use of rulers for practical constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: In practice the conchoid was sometimes not actually drawn; practitioners moved a ruler about the fixed point and adjusted until by trial the intercept equaled the given length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For practical applications where exact curve-drawing is inconvenient, use a physical ruler-and-peg method to find the required intercept experimentally rather than analytically constructing the entire curve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duplication of the cube reduced to two mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: The problem of doubling a cube (construct a similar solid of double volume) is equivalent to finding two mean proportionals x,y between given lines a and b with a:x = x:y = y:b (so that x^3 relates appropriately to a and b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After Hippocrates' reduction, the standard approach in Greek mathematics was to seek two mean proportionals; various constructions (Archytas, Eudoxus, Menaechmus) achieve this by intersecting suitable loci (surfaces or conics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Archytas' three-dimensional construction for two mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Find two mean proportionals by determining a point P as the intersection of three surfaces of revolution: (1) a right cone, (2) a cylinder, and (3) a torus (tore). The intersection yields lengths AP and AM giving the two means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct semicircle revolved into a torus, cylinder on a semicircle base, and a cone generated by revolving a tangent triangle; their mutual intersection P satisfies AC:AP = AP:AM = AM:AB. This is a non-planar (solid) construction demonstrating the need for solids in some classical constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eudoxus' projected-curve method for mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Eudoxus likely used a curvilinear locus (projection of a 3D intersection) whose planar projection meets the given circle at the point M; points on this projected curve can be constructed by auxiliary circle and perpendicular constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tannery suggests Eudoxus' construction could be a projection of Archytas' spatial curve onto the plane of the base circle; analytic expression for the projection leads to an explicit curve (e.g., p = (a cos^2 θ)/cos^2 θ in polar form), allowing many points to be constructed and the intersection with the circle to be found, yielding the required mean proportionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Menaechmus' conic intersections for two mean proportionals
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the two mean proportionals by intersecting two conics: either two parabolas (x^2 = a y and y^2 = b x in suitable coordinate setup) or a parabola and a rectangular hyperbola; the intersection point P yields the required proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the relations x^2 = a y, y^2 = b x, and xy = ab as Cartesian equations of conics; construct those conics (parabola, hyperbola) with appropriate axes/asymptotes and take their intersection to obtain the solution. Eutocius gives analysis and synthesis for both solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quadratrix as a universal angle divider
rubrics_metrics.description: The quadratrix (a special curve) can divide any given angle in a given ratio, and so covers the case of trisection and the construction of regular polygons with sides equal to multiples of nine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quadratrix provides a general means to divide angles by arbitrary rational ratio, but may be less 'practicable' than later conic methods for particular cases like trisection. Historically used to extend constructions beyond straightedge-and-compass limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpret geometrical loci algebraically to identify appropriate curves
rubrics_metrics.description: Translate geometrical proportional conditions (e.g., continued proportion, rectangle equality) into algebraic equations to recognize the conic or higher-degree curve that must be constructed (e.g., parabola for p = k x^2, hyperbola for xy = const).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This analytical viewpoint (used implicitly or explicitly by Menaechmus, Archytas' modern interpreters, and later commentators) helps identify which conic or surface intersection yields the required mean proportionals or angular divisions; it connects geometric construction to algebraic solvability (e.g., cubic equations).
